title: Swiss Glaciers Are Melting Fast — and It's Getting Worse
summary:
Imagine a giant block of ice the size of a mountain. Now imagine it shrinking by more than 5% in a single year. That's what's happening to Switzerland's glaciers — and it's happening fast.

This year, Swiss glaciers lost 5.5% of their total ice volume. That's the second-biggest yearly drop ever recorded. Even worse: over the past five years, they've lost nearly a fifth of their ice. That's like filling 2.2 trillion liters of water — four times what everyone in Switzerland uses in a year.

Why is this happening? Heat waves and low snowfall in winter. Snow is important because it protects the ice below and helps build new ice. Without enough snow, the glaciers can't recover.

"Alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving in the long term under such conditions," experts said.

Scientists are clear about the cause: human-made climate change. "The warming that we are experiencing now can be attributed 100 per cent to anthropogenic climate change," said Matthias Huss, who leads a glacier monitoring group. "Without human emissions or fossil fuels we wouldn't have any warming at the moment."

Switzerland is called the "water tower of Europe" because its glaciers feed major rivers like the Rhine and the Po. If they disappear, it could affect water supplies for millions of people.

But there's still hope for polar ice sheets, Huss said. "There, we can make a difference."
why_it_matters: The water locked in those glaciers flows into rivers that millions of people drink from and farm with, so what happens in the Alps can affect taps and fields far away.

background_read: Glaciers are slow rivers of ice on high mountains. They grow when a lot of snow falls and shrink when summers are hot, because melting ice runs away faster than new snow can pile up.
Switzerland is a small, mountainous country in central Europe, and scientists there have been measuring its glaciers for more than a century.
The Rhine and the Po are big European rivers that get much of their summer water from melting mountain ice, so millions of people, farms and factories rely on that water.
Article_Structure: WHO: Swiss glacier scientists, including Matthias Huss, who leads a glacier monitoring group.
WHAT: Swiss glaciers lost 5.5% of their ice in one year — the second-biggest yearly drop ever recorded — and nearly a fifth of their ice in five years.
WHERE: Switzerland, called the 'water tower of Europe' because its glaciers feed rivers like the Rhine and the Po.
WHY: Human-made climate change is bringing heat waves and low winter snowfall, so the protective snow cover is too thin for the glaciers to rebuild.

perspectives.description: Experts warn that Alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving in the long term under these hot, low-snow conditions.
Scientist Matthias Huss says there is still hope for the polar ice sheets, because there human choices can still make a difference.
People and farms that depend on rivers like the Rhine and the Po could face water shortages if the glaciers keep shrinking.
Measurements show this fits a pattern of very bad years in a row, rather than one strange summer.
